messages.content: What is the periodic table and how is it organised?

The periodic table organises all known chemical elements (118 as of 2023) by their atomic number (number of protons) in order of increasing atomic number, arranged so that elements with similar chemical properties appear in the same column (group). History: Dmitri Mendeleev (1869) arranged elements by atomic mass, leaving gaps for undiscovered elements and predicting their properties with remarkable accuracy (gallium, germanium, scandium were later discovered). Moseley (1913) established that the correct ordering principle is atomic number (protons), not mass. Structure: Periods (rows) — 7 periods. Moving across a period: atomic number increases by 1 each step; electrons are added to the same shell; atomic radius decreases (more protons pull electrons closer); ionisation energy increases; electronegativity increases. Groups (columns): elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons → similar chemical behaviour. Group 1 (alkali metals — Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr): one valence electron; very reactive; form +1 ions. Group 2 (alkaline earth metals — Be, Mg, Ca): two valence electrons; +2 ions. Group 17 (halogens — F, Cl, Br, I): 7 valence electrons; very electronegative; -1 ions. Group 18 (noble gases — He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe): 8 valence electrons (He: 2); extremely unreactive. Transition metals (groups 3-12): d-block; variable oxidation states; form coloured compounds; catalytic activity. Lanthanides and actinides (f-block): bottom rows; 4f and 5f orbital filling. Periodic trends: (1) Atomic radius decreases across period, increases down group. (2) Ionisation energy (energy to remove an electron) increases across period. (3) Electronegativity (tendency to attract electrons in a bond) increases across period and up group — fluorine highest. (4) Electron affinity (energy released when electron added) increases across period.
What are chemical bonds and what are the types?

A chemical bond is the force of attraction that holds atoms together in compounds. Bond type determines physical and chemical properties of materials. Ionic bonds: formed when electrons are transferred from a metal (low electronegativity) to a non-metal (high electronegativity). The resulting oppositely charged ions are held together by electrostatic attraction. NaCl: sodium donates one electron to chlorine → Na⁺ and Cl⁻ lattice. Properties: high melting points (strong lattice), conduct electricity when molten or dissolved (mobile ions), brittle (like charges align under stress). Covalent bonds: formed when electrons are shared between two non-metal atoms. Shared electron pair(s) between nuclei. Single bond: one shared pair (H-H, C-H); double bond: two pairs (C=C, O=O); triple bond: three pairs (N≡N). Bond order: number of shared pairs. Higher bond order → shorter, stronger bond. Polar covalent: electrons shared unequally when atoms have different electronegativities (H₂O, HCl) — the more electronegative atom carries a partial negative charge (δ-). Metallic bonds: free valence electrons delocalised across a lattice of positive metal ions — 'electron sea.' Properties: excellent electrical and thermal conductivity (mobile electrons), lustrous, malleable and ductile (layers of ions can slide without breaking bonds), variable melting points. Hydrogen bonds: strong dipole-dipole interaction between a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to F, O, or N and a lone pair on F, O, or N of another molecule. Strength: ~20 kJ/mol (much weaker than covalent bonds at 200-500 kJ/mol, but stronger than London dispersion forces). Crucial importance: responsible for water's anomalously high boiling point (100°C vs -61°C for H₂S), surface tension, ice floating, and DNA double helix stability. Van der Waals forces: London dispersion (temporary dipoles from electron cloud fluctuations), dipole-dipole, and dipole-induced dipole. Weakest intermolecular forces; increase with molecular size.
What are acids and bases and explain the pH scale?

Acids and bases are defined by three complementary theories of increasing generality. Arrhenius (1884): acid produces H⁺ ions in water; base produces OH⁻. Limited to aqueous systems. Brønsted-Lowry (1923): acid is a proton (H⁺) donor; base is a proton acceptor. Works in non-aqueous systems. HCl + H₂O → Cl⁻ + H₃O⁺: HCl is the acid (donates H⁺), H₂O is the base (accepts H⁺). Conjugate acid-base pairs: HCl/Cl⁻ and H₃O⁺/H₂O. Lewis (1923): acid is an electron pair acceptor; base is an electron pair donor. Most general — explains reactions without proton transfer (BF₃ + NH₃ → F₃B-NH₃: BF₃ is Lewis acid, NH₃ is Lewis base). pH scale: pH = -log₁₀[H⁺] (concentration in mol/L). Water autoionises: Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴ at 25°C. Pure water: [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁷ mol/L → pH = 7 (neutral). Acidic solutions: [H⁺] > [OH⁻]; pH < 7. Basic solutions: [H⁺] < [OH⁻]; pH > 7. The scale is logarithmic: pH 3 is 10× more acidic than pH 4. Strong acids (HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃, HBr, HI, HClO₄): completely dissociate in water — 1M HCl has pH≈0. Weak acids (CH₃COOH, HF, H₂CO₃): partially dissociate; characterised by Ka (acid dissociation constant). pKa = -log Ka; lower pKa = stronger acid. Buffer solutions: resist pH changes upon addition of acid or base; contain a weak acid and its conjugate base (or vice versa). Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]). Biological importance: blood is buffered at pH 7.4 by the carbonic acid-bicarbonate system; enzyme activity is pH-dependent; acid-base disorders (acidosis/alkalosis) are life-threatening.
What is organic chemistry and what are the major functional groups?

Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon-containing compounds — originally thought to require living organisms (Wöhler disproved this in 1828 by synthesising urea). Carbon's unique ability to form 4 stable covalent bonds, to bond to itself in chains and rings, and to form double and triple bonds creates extraordinary molecular diversity (~10 million known organic compounds. Functional groups are specific groups of atoms that confer characteristic chemical properties and reactivity. Major functional groups: Alkanes (C-C and C-H only; no functional group): saturated hydrocarbons; low reactivity; undergo combustion and halogenation. Alkenes (C=C): undergo addition reactions (electrophilic addition — Markovnikov's rule: nucleophile adds to carbon with more hydrogen); polymerisation. Alkynes (C≡C): highly reactive; similar to alkenes. Aromatic (benzene ring): resonance-stabilised; undergo electrophilic aromatic substitution (rather than addition). Alcohols (-OH): hydrogen bonding → high boiling points; weak acids; undergo oxidation (primary → aldehyde → carboxylic acid; secondary → ketone), substitution, and elimination. Aldehydes (-CHO) and Ketones (-C=O-): carbonyl group; undergo nucleophilic addition; aldehydes are easily oxidised to carboxylic acids. Carboxylic acids (-COOH): weak acids; form esters and amides; undergo decarboxylation. Esters (-COO-): formed from alcohol + acid; fruity smells; undergo hydrolysis. Amines (-NH₂, -NHR, -NR₂): basic (lone pair on N); nucleophilic. Amides (-CONH-): peptide bond is an amide; stable; require harsh conditions to hydrolyse. Thiols (-SH): analogous to alcohols but more acidic; important in proteins (cysteine). Halides (-F, -Cl, -Br, -I): undergo nucleophilic substitution (SN1/SN2) and elimination.
What is thermochemistry and what are enthalpy and entropy?

Thermochemistry studies heat changes in chemical reactions. Enthalpy (H): the heat content of a system at constant pressure. The enthalpy change ΔH = H_products - H_reactants. Exothermic reactions release heat (ΔH < 0 — products at lower energy than reactants): combustion, neutralisation, respiration. Endothermic reactions absorb heat (ΔH > 0): photosynthesis, dissolving ammonium nitrate, decomposition. Hess's Law: the enthalpy change for a reaction is the same regardless of the pathway — because enthalpy is a state function (depends only on initial and final states). This allows calculation of ΔH for reactions that cannot be measured directly by combining known ΔH values. Standard enthalpy of formation ΔH°f: enthalpy change when 1 mole of a compound is formed from its constituent elements in their standard states. ΔH°reaction = Σ ΔH°f(products) - Σ ΔH°f(elements and compounds formed in reaction). Bond enthalpies: approximate ΔH by summing bonds broken (endothermic) minus bonds formed (exothermic). Entropy (S): thermodynamic measure of disorder or the number of accessible microstates. Reactions that increase disorder (gas production from solids or liquids, more product molecules than reactant, dissolution) have positive ΔS. Gibbs free energy: G = H - TS. ΔG = ΔH - TΔS at constant temperature and pressure. If ΔG < 0: reaction is spontaneous (thermodynamically favourable). If ΔG > 0: non-spontaneous. If ΔG = 0: at equilibrium. Implications: (1) Exothermic reactions with entropy increase (ΔH<0, ΔS>0): spontaneous at all temperatures. (2) Endothermic with entropy decrease (ΔH>0, ΔS<0): never spontaneous. (3) Mixed cases: temperature determines spontaneity. ΔG = -RT ln K: the equilibrium constant K is related to the standard free energy change.
What is electrochemistry and how do batteries work?

Electrochemistry studies the interconversion of chemical and electrical energy through redox reactions at electrode surfaces. Redox reactions involve transfer of electrons: oxidation (loss of electrons — OIL) and reduction (gain of electrons — RIG). A galvanic (voltaic) cell converts spontaneous chemical energy to electrical energy. Structure: two half-cells connected by a salt bridge and external circuit. Anode: oxidation occurs; negative terminal in galvanic cell. Cathode: reduction occurs; positive terminal. Salt bridge: allows ion flow to maintain electrical neutrality without allowing bulk mixing of solutions. Daniell cell (classic example): Zn anode (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻) and Cu cathode (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu). Standard EMF = E°cathode - E°anode = +0.34 - (-0.76) = +1.10V. ΔG = -nFE where n = moles of electrons transferred, F = Faraday constant (96,485 C/mol), E = cell EMF. Spontaneous cells have E > 0 and ΔG < 0. Nernst equation: E = E° - (RT/nF)ln Q — corrects for non-standard concentrations. Modern batteries: Lithium-ion (Li-ion): graphite anode (lithium ions intercalate between graphite layers), lithium cobalt oxide cathode. Li⁺ ions shuttle between electrodes; electrons flow through the external circuit. High energy density, rechargeable (thousands of cycles). Used in phones, laptops, EVs. Lead-acid battery: Pb anode (Pb → PbSO₄ + 2e⁻), PbO₂ cathode (PbO₂ + 4H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ + 2e⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2H₂O). 2V per cell; 12V car batteries have 6 cells. Rechargeable; high current discharge; heavy. Electrolysis: non-spontaneous redox driven by external electricity — water splitting (2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂), chlor-alkali process (NaCl → Cl₂ + NaOH + H₂), electroplating.
What is chemical kinetics and what factors affect reaction rates?

Chemical kinetics studies the rates of chemical reactions — how fast reactants are converted to products and what factors control this rate. Reaction rate: typically expressed as the rate of change of concentration of a reactant or product with time. Rate = -d[A]/dt = k[A]^m[B]^n. Rate law: the experimentally determined equation relating rate to reactant concentrations. Order of reaction: m+n (sum of exponents in the rate law) — must be determined experimentally, not from stoichiometry. Rate constant k: depends on temperature (Arrhenius equation) but not concentration. Factors affecting rate: (1) Concentration: for most reactions, higher concentration → more frequent collisions → faster rate. Zero order: rate independent of [A]. First order: rate = k[A] (half-life = 0.693/k — constant regardless of concentration; radioactive decay, many drug metabolism reactions). Second order: rate = k[A]². (2) Temperature: Arrhenius equation: k = A·e^{-Ea/RT} where A = pre-exponential factor (collision frequency × orientation factor), Ea = activation energy (minimum energy required for reaction), R = gas constant, T = absolute temperature. As T increases, more molecules have energy ≥ Ea → exponential increase in rate. Rule of thumb: rate approximately doubles for every 10°C rise. (3) Catalysts: lower the activation energy by providing an alternative reaction pathway — increase rate without being consumed. Homogeneous (same phase as reactants) vs. heterogeneous (different phase — surface catalysis, e.g., Pt in catalytic converters). Enzymes: biological catalysts — extraordinarily specific and efficient. (4) Surface area: for solid reactants, greater surface area → more exposure → faster reaction. (5) Light: photochemical reactions (chlorine + methane requires UV light to initiate radical chain mechanism). Collision theory: reactions occur when molecules collide with sufficient energy and correct orientation.
What is the mole concept and Avogadro's number?

The mole (mol) is the SI unit of amount of substance. One mole contains exactly 6.02214076×10²³ entities (atoms, molecules, ions, electrons, or any specified particle) — Avogadro's constant NA = 6.022×10²³ mol⁻¹. The mole bridges the macroscopic world (grams we can measure) and the microscopic world (atoms and molecules we cannot directly count). Molar mass: the mass of one mole of a substance, expressed in g/mol, numerically equal to the relative atomic/molecular mass (in amu). H₂O: molar mass = 2(1.008) + 16.00 = 18.02 g/mol. This means 18.02 g of water contains 6.022×10²³ molecules of H₂O. Mole calculations: n = m/M (moles = mass / molar mass); n = N/NA (moles = number of particles / Avogadro's number); for ideal gases: n = PV/RT. Stoichiometry: balanced chemical equations specify molar ratios. N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃: 1 mol N₂ reacts with 3 mol H₂ to produce 2 mol NH₃. Given 28g N₂: n(N₂) = 28/28 = 1 mol → produces 2 mol NH₃ = 2×17 = 34g NH₃ and consumes 3 mol H₂ = 6g H₂. Empirical formula from combustion analysis: burn compound, measure CO₂ and H₂O produced; calculate moles of C and H; determine simplest ratio. Molecular formula: multiply empirical formula by integer if molar mass is known. Avogadro's law (for ideal gases): equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of moles. Standard molar volume at STP (0°C, 1 atm): 22.4 L/mol. The historical determination of NA used methods including oil film thickness estimation, Millikan's oil drop experiment, X-ray crystallography of ionic crystals, and Brownian motion.
What is nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and how does it work?

NMR spectroscopy is one of the most powerful analytical techniques in chemistry, providing detailed information about molecular structure, dynamics, and environment by exploiting the magnetic properties of certain atomic nuclei. Physical basis: certain nuclei have non-zero nuclear spin (quantum property): ¹H, ¹³C, ³¹P, ¹⁹F, ¹⁵N are NMR-active (the most important being ¹H). When placed in a strong external magnetic field B₀, nuclear spins align parallel (lower energy, α state) or antiparallel (higher energy, β state). The energy difference: ΔE = γ·ℏ·B₀ where γ is the gyromagnetic ratio (nucleus-specific). ΔE corresponds to radiofrequency (RF) electromagnetic radiation. Resonance: a pulse of RF radiation at the Larmor frequency ν = γ·B₀/(2π) flips spins from α to β. When they relax back, they emit RF radiation detected by the spectrometer. Chemical shift: the precise resonance frequency depends on the electronic environment of the nucleus (electronegative groups deshield, reducing the local field; electron donation shields). Chemical shift δ (in ppm relative to TMS = 0): aromatic and vinyl protons (6-9 ppm), aldehyde CHO (~10 ppm), carboxylic OH (~10-12 ppm), C-H adjacent to carbonyl (2-3 ppm), alkyl C-H (0-3 ppm). Coupling constants (J): neighbouring protons (through bonds) split each other's signals — n+1 rule (proton with n equivalent neighbours splits into n+1 peaks). ¹H-¹H coupling reveals connectivity. Integration: peak area is proportional to the number of equivalent protons — determines relative proton counts. 2D NMR (COSY, HSQC, HMBC): shows correlations between coupled nuclei, revealing connectivity. MRI: medical imaging uses ¹H NMR of water in body tissues — spatial encoding by magnetic field gradients.
What are polymers and how are they made?

Polymers are large molecules (macromolecules) composed of many repeating structural units (monomers) linked by covalent bonds. The word comes from Greek: 'poly' (many) + 'meros' (part). Natural polymers include proteins (amino acid monomers), DNA/RNA (nucleotide monomers), cellulose and starch (glucose monomers), and rubber (isoprene monomers). Synthetic polymers are one of the most important classes of materials. Polymerisation reactions: Addition (chain-growth) polymerisation: monomers containing double bonds (alkenes) add sequentially to a growing chain. The double bond opens; no atoms are lost as by-products. Steps: initiation (creation of a reactive radical, cation, or anion), propagation (successive monomer addition), termination (chain ends). Examples: polyethylene (PE) from ethylene CH₂=CH₂; polypropylene (PP) from propylene; polyvinyl chloride (PVC) from vinyl chloride; polystyrene (PS) from styrene; polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE/Teflon) from tetrafluoroethylene. Condensation (step-growth) polymerisation: monomers react, expelling a small molecule (typically water or HCl) in each step. Requires monomers with two functional groups (bifunctional). Nylon 6,6: hexamethylenediamine (H₂N-(CH₂)₆-NH₂) + adipic acid (HOOC-(CH₂)₄-COOH) → nylon + H₂O. Polyester (PET): ethylene glycol + terephthalic acid → PET + H₂O. Polycarbonate: diphenol + carbonyl chloride. Polymer properties depend on chain length (degree of polymerisation), branching, cross-linking, and tacticity (spatial arrangement of side groups — isotactic, syndiotactic, atactic). Thermosets (epoxies, vulcanised rubber) are heavily cross-linked and cannot be remelted; thermoplastics (PET, PE) soften on heating and can be reprocessed.
Explain atomic structure — how atoms are built and what determines element properties.

ATOMIC STRUCTURE — The Building Blocks of Matter

THE ATOM:
Discovered to have internal structure in early 20th century.
Nucleus: protons (positive charge) + neutrons (no charge). Very dense, tiny.
Electrons: negative charge, orbit nucleus in shells/orbitals. Most of atom is empty space.

Nuclear dimensions: if atom were a football stadium, nucleus would be a marble at centre.

SUBATOMIC PARTICLES:
Proton: mass 1.67×10^-27 kg, charge +1, symbol p+
Neutron: mass 1.67×10^-27 kg, charge 0, symbol n
Electron: mass 9.11×10^-31 kg (1/1836 of proton), charge -1, symbol e-

ATOMIC NUMBER AND MASS:
Atomic number (Z): number of protons. DEFINES the element. Carbon always has 6 protons.
Mass number (A): protons + neutrons.
Isotopes: same element (same Z), different neutrons.
 Carbon-12: 6p + 6n (stable, 98.9% of carbon)
 Carbon-13: 6p + 7n (stable, 1.1%)
 Carbon-14: 6p + 8n (radioactive! used in carbon dating)

ELECTRON SHELLS (Bohr model — simplified):
Electrons occupy shells (n=1,2,3...) at increasing energies.
Shell capacity: 2n² electrons. Shell 1: 2, Shell 2: 8, Shell 3: 18.
Valence electrons: outermost shell. Determine chemical reactivity.

Sodium (Na): 11 electrons. Configuration: 2, 8, 1. ONE valence electron.
Chlorine (Cl): 17 electrons. Configuration: 2, 8, 7. SEVEN valence electrons.
Na + Cl: Na gives its 1 valence electron to Cl -> both achieve full outer shell.
Result: Na+ and Cl- ions -> ionic bond -> NaCl (table salt).

QUANTUM MECHANICAL MODEL (real):
Electrons don''t orbit in circles — they exist in probability clouds (orbitals).
Orbital types: s (sphere), p (dumbbell), d (complex), f (very complex).
Pauli exclusion: max 2 electrons per orbital (opposite spins).
Aufbau: fill lowest energy orbitals first.
Hund''s rule: single electron in each orbital before pairing.

Carbon: 1s² 2s² 2p² (4 valence electrons -> forms 4 bonds -> basis of organic chemistry)
Neon: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ (full outer shell -> noble gas -> chemically inert)

THE PERIODIC TABLE:
Organised by atomic number (left to right, top to bottom).
Groups (columns): same number of valence electrons -> similar chemistry.
Periods (rows): same number of electron shells.
Trends:
 Atomic radius: increases down (more shells), decreases right (more protons pull electrons in).
 Electronegativity: increases up and right. Fluorine most electronegative.
 Ionisation energy: energy to remove an electron. Increases up and right.
Explain chemical bonding — ionic, covalent, and metallic bonds.

CHEMICAL BONDS — how atoms join together.

IONIC BONDS:
Transfer of electrons from metal to nonmetal.
Sodium (2,8,1): gives 1 electron -> Na+ (stable, full outer shell).
Chlorine (2,8,7): gains 1 electron -> Cl- (stable, full outer shell).
Opposite charges attract: NaCl (sodium chloride = table salt).

Properties: high melting points (strong electrostatic forces), conduct electricity when dissolved.
Crystal lattice: 3D repeating structure of alternating positive and negative ions.

COVALENT BONDS:
Sharing of electron pairs between nonmetals.
H₂: two hydrogen atoms share 1 pair of electrons. Single bond.
O₂: oxygen atoms share 2 pairs. Double bond. Stronger, shorter.
N₂: nitrogen atoms share 3 pairs. Triple bond. Very strong (nitrogen is inert gas).

Polar covalent: unequal sharing due to different electronegativities.
H₂O: O is more electronegative -> pulls electrons -> partial negative on O, positive on H.
Result: polar molecule with partial charges (δ+ and δ-).

Nonpolar covalent: equal sharing. O₂, N₂, CH₄ (carbon and hydrogen similar electronegativity).

METALLIC BONDS:
Positive metal ions in "sea of delocalised electrons."
Electrons free to move -> good electrical and thermal conductors.
Ions can slide -> metals malleable and ductile (don''t shatter like ionic crystals).

INTERMOLECULAR FORCES (between molecules, weaker):
Hydrogen bond: H bonded to N, O, or F -> strong dipole -> attracts other molecules.
 Water: high boiling point, surface tension, ice less dense than water -> all due to H-bonds.
Van der Waals (London dispersion): temporary dipoles in all molecules. Weak.
 Noble gases, hydrocarbons: interact only via VdW. Low boiling points.
 Geckos: millions of tiny hairs exploit VdW to walk on walls.
Explain acids, bases, and pH.

ACIDS AND BASES

ARRHENIUS DEFINITION:
Acid: produces H+ ions in water. HCl -> H+ + Cl-.
Base: produces OH- ions in water. NaOH -> Na+ + OH-.

BRONSTED-LOWRY (broader):
Acid: proton (H+) donor.
Base: proton acceptor.
HCl + H₂O -> H₃O+ + Cl- (HCl donates proton to water).
NH₃ + H₂O -> NH₄+ + OH- (NH₃ accepts proton from water).

LEWIS (broadest):
Acid: electron pair acceptor.
Base: electron pair donor.

pH:
pH = -log[H+] (concentration of H+ ions in mol/L).
pH 0-7: acidic. pH 7: neutral (pure water at 25°C). pH 7-14: basic (alkaline).
Each unit = 10× difference in [H+].
pH 3 is 100× more acidic than pH 5.
pOH = -log[OH-]. pH + pOH = 14.

COMMON VALUES:
Stomach acid: pH 1-2. Lemon juice: pH 2. Vinegar: pH 3. Coffee: pH 5.
Milk: pH 6.5. Blood: pH 7.4 (tightly regulated — 7.35-7.45). Sea water: pH 8.1.
Baking soda: pH 9. Ammonia: pH 11. Bleach: pH 13.

STRONG vs WEAK:
Strong acids: fully dissociate. HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄, HBr, HI, HClO₄.
Weak acids: partially dissociate. CH₃COOH (acetic acid), H₂CO₃ (carbonic), HF.
 Ka: acid dissociation constant. Larger Ka = stronger acid.

NEUTRALISATION:
Acid + Base -> Salt + Water.
HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H₂O.
H₂SO₄ + 2KOH -> K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O.

BUFFERS:
Resist pH change. Contain weak acid and its conjugate base.
Blood buffer: H₂CO₃ / HCO₃- (carbonic acid / bicarbonate).
If acid added: HCO₃- neutralises it. If base added: H₂CO₃ neutralises it.
pH stays ~7.4 despite small additions of acid or base.
Explain organic chemistry — functional groups and reactions.

ORGANIC CHEMISTRY — carbon-based compounds.

Carbon is special: 4 bonds, chains up to millions of atoms, ring structures, double bonds.

HYDROCARBONS (only C and H):
Alkanes: only single bonds. CH₄ methane, C₂H₆ ethane, C₃H₈ propane. General: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
 Saturated. Used as fuels.
Alkenes: one double bond. C₂H₄ ethylene, C₃H₆ propylene. CₙH₂ₙ.
 Unsaturated. More reactive. Basis of plastics (polyethylene = many ethylene units).
Alkynes: triple bond. C₂H₂ acetylene. Very reactive.
Aromatics: benzene ring (C₆H₆). Delocalized electrons. Stable. Basis of drugs, dyes.

FUNCTIONAL GROUPS (determine chemical properties):
Alcohol (-OH): ethanol C₂H₅OH. Polar, soluble in water. Combustible.
Aldehyde (-CHO): formaldehyde HCHO. Reactive. Preservative.
Ketone (-CO-): acetone (CH₃)₂CO. Solvent.
Carboxylic acid (-COOH): acetic acid CH₃COOH (vinegar). Acidic.
Ester (-COO-): formed from acid + alcohol. Fragrant (fruit flavours, perfumes).
Amine (-NH₂): amino acids, DNA bases. Basic (alkaline).
Amide (-CONH-): peptide bond links amino acids. Nylon is a polyamide.

KEY REACTIONS:
Esterification: RCOOH + R''OH -> RCOOR'' + H₂O. Acid + alcohol -> ester + water.
Saponification: ester + base -> acid salt + alcohol. Making soap from fat + NaOH.
Polymerisation: small monomers link to form polymer.
 Addition: ethylene -> polyethylene (plastic bags).
 Condensation: releases H₂O with each link (nylon, polyester, proteins).
Substitution (alkanes): CH₄ + Cl₂ -> CH₃Cl + HCl (in UV light).
Addition (alkenes): C₂H₄ + H₂ -> C₂H₆ (hydrogenation — makes margarine from vegetable oil).
How does organic synthesis work — retrosynthesis and reaction planning?

ORGANIC SYNTHESIS — making target molecules from available starting materials.

RETROSYNTHESIS (disconnection approach — Corey):
Work backwards from target molecule.
Identify bonds to disconnect -> simpler precursors.
Continue until reach available starting materials.
Arrow (=>) means "can be made from" (retrosynthetic).

Example: making ethyl acetate (CH₃COOC₂H₅):
 Target: ethyl acetate
 Disconnect ester: => acetic acid (CH₃COOH) + ethanol (C₂H₅OH)
 Both available. Reaction: Fischer esterification with acid catalyst.

REACTION TYPES:
Oxidation: increases oxidation state. Primary alcohol -> aldehyde -> carboxylic acid.
 Reagents: PCC (to aldehyde), KMnO₄/K₂Cr₂O₇ (to acid).
Reduction: decreases oxidation state. Ketone -> secondary alcohol.
 Reagents: NaBH₄ (mild), LiAlH₄ (strong), H₂/Pd.
Grignard reaction: RMgBr + carbonyl -> alcohol. Carbon-carbon bond formation!
 CH₃MgBr + formaldehyde -> CH₃CH₂OH (after workup).
 Key: making C-C bonds to build carbon skeleton.
Aldol condensation: two carbonyl compounds -> beta-hydroxy carbonyl.
 Important: C-C bond forming with alpha-carbon of one carbonyl attacking another.

PROTECTING GROUPS:
If molecule has two reactive functional groups, protect one while reacting the other.
Hydroxyl protection: convert -OH to -OTBDMS (silyl ether), react elsewhere, deprotect.
Amine protection: -NH₂ -> -NHBoc (with Boc₂O), react elsewhere, deprotect with acid.

GREEN CHEMISTRY (minimising waste):
12 principles: prevent waste, atom economy (use all atoms in product), less hazardous reagents.
Atom economy = MW(desired product) / MW(all products) × 100%.
Addition reactions: 100% atom economy (all atoms end up in product).
Substitution: lower atom economy (leaving group becomes waste).
